Then, I realised that if I were to go to court, the officer could say I told him I researched what to do when talking to police before he talked to me. That looks incriminating. Crazy stuff.

Thing is, when you're innocent anyway, it's kind of against my nature, and I suspect a lot of folks feel the same, to refuse to offer your input if asked... Because you hope that your input will help with finding the guilty party.

Personally, I fell into this a couple of years ago when some camera equipment was stolen at my work. It was taken from a "secure" room and I had been one of the few folks who had accessed the room legitimately in the hours before the theft was discovered. My access had been recorded when I used my prox card ID to unlock the door. Naturally, the police wanted to talk to me and, having nothing to hide, I was happy to meet with them.

I also felt that they should know that while I had used my prox card to open the door it was entirely possible to gain entry to the room without using a card so I went to the interview intending to discuss this with them. They were exceedingly interested in how and why I knew the room could be accessed without using a prox card: I know there are master keys that override the electronic lock, I know that power issues can cause the doors to unlock and be leveraged to deliberately unlock a door, I know that the lock can be opened with strong magnets... Because I've had legitimate reasons to access other rooms when there's been a fault with the prox locks. Never mind the fact that that particular door doesn't self-close correctly... You have to pull it shut behind you or the lock doesn't always click in.

And when they asked me about my knowledge of the other people that had been recorded as entering the room, I knew two of them as colleagues and they asked me for a personal opinions of them... One of them had suffered a number of strokes in the past and as a result often didn't grasp details too well anymore, sometimes became confused, and sometimes simply misspoke. I, in an attempt to give him a break, as well as to offer some advice to the police when speaking to him, explained that it was best to take it easy with him... And hey presto, now I'm a suspect with an accomplice. FML. They didn't outright accuse me, but it was obvious they suspected me and they asked me straight if I'd done it and, I don't know why, but I felt panic and guilt when that happened.

In the end, I don't know what happened, if they found the thief or the equipment, but I heard no more from the police so I guess my panic was unjustified. However, I spent several sleepless nights wondering if I had incriminated myself unintentionally and was about to be arrested for something I had no hand in. More so, I worried that my colleague was going to be accused and that it would be explained that I implicated him. It could easily have gone differently because of my actions, but I was honestly trying to help.

Next time... Next time I'll just keep my mouth shut.

That's the thing, isn't it? You want to help. You might be an important witness. They're interested in the information that you have, because you might be an expert or at least that's what you think... but suddenly you end up incriminating yourself.

It's easy to say never to talk to the police, but sometimes you just don't even consider that they might find you to be a suspect. And that's why it's so important to hammer in this message.
Of course you won't usually have that much bad luck.. but maybe you have and then you'll regret it.

Exactly. I was trying to help but felt entirely like I lead them into suspecting me and my colleague.

But, yes, saying I would keep quiet in future isn't that realistic. Maybe if was a similarly "small" crime... The value of the stolen items wasn't high, the equipment insured (though I'm sure there was a deductible to pay), the victim an organization rather than an individual... But otherwise I guess I would still feel compelled to give my input, though I think I would be very guarded about what I say.

But even that would worry me. Being guarded would probably seem suspicious. Having a lawyer present would definitely be the option I'd choose in the future.

Fun fact: In Canada, nobody has the right to have a lawyer present during questioning. You have the right to consult before questioning, but not during.
